evidence: The comment at src/sqllens/memory/io.py:30-34 says MAX_BUNDLE_DEPTH=64 stays far below the depth where json.loads on 3.11 raises RecursionError (under 1,000 levels). On CPython 3.11 the C scanner calls Py_EnterRecursiveCall, which shares the interpreter recursion limit (default 1000) with Python frames. So json.loads of deeply nested arrays fails at roughly 1,000 levels minus the current stack depth. The older '5-9k' figure matches 3.12+, where C recursion is counted separately. 64 is far below 1,000. Hostile input: a bundle nested 500 deep. The 64 cap rejects it first. I did not run Python here; this rests on my knowledge of CPython 3.11 internals, not on a run.

parse_json (io.py:137) calls json.loads(text) with no object_hook, object_pairs_hook, parse_* or cls arguments. The default decoder yields only dict, list, str, int, float, bool and None, so dict and list are the only containers. _enforce_depth_cap (io.py:98-113) pushes only dict/list children, so no other container type can evade the depth count. Subclasses are also covered by isinstance, and the absolute claim's hostile input (a deep nested array or object) is walked correctly.

io.py:98-113 _enforce_depth_cap pops every container from an explicit heap list and iterates all its children, pushing each dict/list child; it is called unconditionally at io.py:148 after json.loads and before validation. So it visits every container and examines every child: time is O(graph), and the explicit stack (heap, not call stack) can hold up to the number of containers, so extra memory is also proportional to the graph. For a valid 10,000-item bundle (MAX_BUNDLE_ITEMS = 10_000, schema.py:41) it walks all items. The claim is descriptive and matches the code.

Depth rejection raises BundleFormatError (io.py:109) and RecursionError is converted to BundleFormatError (io.py:140-145), same type as other parse failures. server.py:429-431 catches BundleFormatError and raises RuntimeError('Invalid memory bundle: ...'), which FastMCP surfaces as isError. cli.py:458-461 catches it and exits with code 1. Minor: the CLI prefix is 'Invalid bundle:' rather than 'Invalid memory bundle:', but the handling matches that of every other parse failure.

io.py:146-150: _enforce_depth_cap(raw) runs before the root check. It (io.py:98-113) only raises when container depth exceeds MAX_BUNDLE_DEPTH=64 (io.py:34). Shallow non-object roots such as [], 42, null, "x" have depth <=1 (or no containers), so no raise, and control reaches the unchanged 'bundle root must be a JSON object' at line 150. Only roots nested >64 deep change message, and those could not have been previously-tested shallow cases. No Python test in the head view asserts the root-type text (grep of *.py), so no existing assertion is contradicted.

src/sqllens/memory/io.py:14 does `import json` (stdlib module, no alias). tests/unit/test_memory_schema_io.py:13 imports io as memory_io, so memory_io.json is the global stdlib json module object. monkeypatch.setattr(obj, name, value) sets the attribute on that object (visible to all importers) and undoes it at test teardown per pytest semantics.

Depth check at io.py:108 only rejects depth > 64, so depth-64 payloads pass it. _nested_arrays(64) gives a list root, so io.py:149-150 raises BundleFormatError('bundle root must be a JSON object'). _object_over_arrays(64) has depth 1 + 63 = 64 and root {'x':...}. _nested_objects(64) has root {'a':...}. Both go to MemoryBundle.model_validate (io.py:152), which has extra='forbid' (schema.py:100). The unknown keys x and a raise ValidationError, which is wrapped as BundleFormatError (io.py:154). Each shape therefore raises a non-depth BundleFormatError, as the comment says.

_enforce_depth_cap (src/sqllens/memory/io.py:98-113) starts the root at depth 1. _object_over_arrays(d) (tests/unit/test_memory_schema_io.py:140-141) is a root object (1) wrapping _nested_arrays(d-1), which has d-1 array levels, so the total is d. _nested_objects(d) (144-145) repeats '{"a": ' d times, giving d nested objects, so the total is d. Both are valid JSON and match the cap's convention for d>=1.

Payload (test_memory_schema_io.py:181-184): root dict depth 1; sql_pairs is first key (shallow); schema_docs is the second key, a list at depth 2 whose second item is _nested_arrays(64) (line 136-137: 64 nested '[' ). That starts at depth 3 and its deepest container is depth 66 > MAX_BUNDLE_DEPTH=64 (io.py:34). _enforce_depth_cap (io.py:98-113) raises when depth > 64. The first list item and first key are shallow, so a first-child-only walk would miss it. Comment matches.

parse_json (src/sqllens/memory/io.py:134-156) calls json.loads first; a JSONDecodeError is mapped to 'invalid JSON: ...' (line 138-139) before _enforce_depth_cap (line 148) can run. Counterexample: a file of 100 '[' characters (unclosed, nesting >64 but below recursion limit) raises JSONDecodeError and is rejected with 'invalid JSON', not the 'too deeply nested' message. The doc's 'a deeper file is rejected with ...' is therefore not true for every deeper file. Valid-JSON deep files do get the depth message (line 148, and RecursionError arm at 140-145). The doc says the limit affects 'malformed files', which includes such inputs.

parse_json (io.py:134-156) catches RecursionError from json.loads and raises BundleFormatError(_TOO_DEEP_MESSAGE) (140-145); otherwise parsed output goes through the iterative _enforce_depth_cap (98-113, MAX_BUNDLE_DEPTH=64, root=depth 1), run before the root-type check (148). So input just over 64 levels, and a crafted extreme depth (e.g. 100000 levels that overflows json.loads on any version), both give the same message. golden.py:51 sends JSON golden files through parse_json; CSV goes to parse_csv, but the claim is about JSON files so CSV is outside its scope. The size cap is checked first, but that only applies to oversized text and is not a depth case.

schema.py:33,41 define MAX_BUNDLE_BYTES and MAX_BUNDLE_ITEMS; io.py:34 defines MAX_BUNDLE_DEPTH. io.py enforces them via _enforce_size_cap (calls at 135,165), _enforce_depth_cap (148), _enforce_item_caps (155,198). schema.py Field constraints (lines 60,61,80,89,119) are only per-field limits, none use the bundle caps. admin.py:243 also checks MAX_BUNDLE_ITEMS, but that is an extra in-process check and does not contradict that io.py enforces all three at the parse boundary.

io.py: only call site of _enforce_depth_cap is parse_json line 148, after json.loads (137) and before root-type check (149). Walk is iterative with an explicit stack (103-113), root container at depth 1, dicts and lists both counted, raises when depth > 64. RecursionError from json.loads is caught at 140-145 and mapped to BundleFormatError(_TOO_DEEP_MESSAGE), same message as the cap. Hostile input considered: deep array root, which gets the depth error rather than the root-type error.

io.py:98-113 _enforce_depth_cap rejects containers deeper than MAX_BUNDLE_DEPTH=64 (io.py:34) with BundleFormatError, called from parse_json at io.py:148. Hostile input: a very deep JSON nest raises RecursionError in json.loads, caught at io.py:140-145 and converted to BundleFormatError, so it also takes the same arm. Size cap (io.py:49-72) and item caps (io.py:75-95, called at 155) also raise BundleFormatError. server.py:428-431 import_memory catches BundleFormatError and raises RuntimeError(f"Invalid memory bundle: {exc}"); an exception raised from a FastMCP tool surfaces as an isError result.

criteria.json read, criterion 2 matches this claim, so it counts. load_golden (src/sqllens/eval/golden.py:51) calls parse_json(text) for fmt json. The 10,000-level payload is about 20KB, under MAX_BUNDLE_BYTES = 10 MiB (memory/schema.py:33), so the size cap does not fire. parse_json (memory/io.py:134-150) has three outcomes. (1) json.loads raises RecursionError: converted to BundleFormatError(_TOO_DEEP_MESSAGE) ('...too deeply nested...'). (2) json.loads succeeds, as on interpreters with no recursion limit in the C scanner: _enforce_depth_cap (io.py:98-113) walks iteratively and raises the same message at depth > 64, before the root-type check at line 149. (3) JSONDecodeError cannot occur because the payload is well-formed. CI unit matrix is 3.11-3.14 (ci.yml:38). Test test_load_golden_inherits_recursion_guard (tests/unit/test_eval_golden.py:82-90) asserts match 'deeply nested' for this payload through load_golden. Trigger alternatives split: JSONDecodeError branch -> outside the trigger (payload is well-formed); RecursionError branch -> yields the required message; size-cap branch -> outside the trigger (payload far below cap); non-dict root check -> runs after the depth cap, so it is never reached. I did not run the tests on each interpreter, so the per-version claim rests on tracing both json.loads outcomes.
